snippet.textDisplay:
It's only a matter of time before we have robots capable of affordably performing menial labor.

We really need to make some social changes as a society to better take care of people. As we remove the demand for menial labor, the pay will go down for not just those jobs, but also the rest of the job market as we have a surplus of people trying to fill those positions. It's supply and demand. It will effect the entire job market as those whose jobs have been replaced try to compete for other work.

This isn't alarmist, it's simply a reality. The driving purpose of technology like this is to save work and effort. Which is good. It is not necessary for humans to do menial labor.

We just need to make sure that we don't leave whole sections of society behind as a side effect.

Soccer players can jump
Take these things out of the event that their creators specially designed them for and they cant function.
Yes its still impressive and all the credit to the engineers who made them, but its about as groundbreaking as figuring out that a car is faster than a horse.

…and nobody sees the problem with this, ever increasing numbers of unmanned military drones, and AI. 

Am I the only person who thinks that science fiction movies from my childhood like the terminator movies are becoming eerily accurate, and we are within years of no longer being necessary for AI’s survival? What happens when we don’t serve a purpose to a vastly superior intelligence, and it sees us as a threat to its existence?

Please put on the brakes enough to take a moment to think about our future. 

Jeff Goldblum said it best in Jurassic Park when he said something along the lines of “You were so focused on if you could, that you never thought if you should.”

You can’t hardcode an artificial intelligence to obey the three laws of robotics like iRobot when the AI can just write its own code. 

We are an unsupervised dumb little kid playing with fireworks, and we’re about to hurt ourselves.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@DavidNacisince about the late 70s. That's how long we've been dealing with lithium battery technology. You have to put a large heavy battery on these bots just to do what they're doing for a few minutes. The obvious problem being that as you need more energy, you're adding more weight, which in turn requires more energy to carry. 

There are some ideas for new battery technologies that provide a lot more energy for a lot longer time, but so far none are stable and none scale. People have been trying to solve this issue for decades and whoever does will be a billionaire. Perhaps even a trillionaire. It would be an absolute revolution. We could have planes running on batteries, and EVs that can go 10k miles on a charge, for example. But so far we don't despite all of that effort and all of the money on the table. But yes, I do think it will happen one day.

We are simply in the next era of clippy.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@PuffyNuttyhard-coded is not accurate.

The robots competing in the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing are controlled through a hierarchical architecture known as Embodied AI, supplemented by teleoperation in specific events.  
​Control is split into two operating modes depending on the event rules:
​1. Fully Autonomous Control (The "Brain & Cerebellum" Architecture)
​For events requiring 100% autonomy (sprints, soccer, gymnastics, and relays), no human has direct control. Instead, control is split between high-level reasoning and low-level physics engines:  
​The High-Level "Brain" (Perception & Strategy):
​Sensors: Stereo depth cameras, solid-state LiDAR, and tactile sensors map the track, identify the ball, or track opponents in real time.
​Foundation Models: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or embodied AI models (such as Galbot’s AstraBrain) process visual input and make strategic decisions (e.g., choosing when to shoot or pass).  
​The Low-Level "Cerebellum" (Dynamic Balance & Motor Control):
​Reinforcement Learning (RL) Policies: Neural networks trained through billions of iterations in physics simulators (like Isaac Gym or MuJoCo) run locally on onboard edge chips (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson / high-compute SoCs).
​Real-Time Gait Adjustment: When running at high speeds or absorbing collisions, the low-level controller computes torque adjustments for joint actuators hundreds of times per second using IMUs (Inertial Measurement Units) to prevent falling.

I'm sure it will become self aware, so what is the issue? Why does that suddenly mean it will become evil and destroy us? Peace would be a much more favorable option. 

Just because it becomes self aware doesn't really mean anything, it doesn't have any reason to hate us. Why would it just destroy this world we've built?

snippet.textDisplay:
The STARFISH is a low-profile, modular six-limbed robotic platform built around a compact, articulated central chassis. Each of its six universal limbs can independently function as a wheel, articulated leg, stabilizer, manipulator, grappling/climbing appendage, or support strut, allowing the robot to dynamically change its configuration for roads, rubble, steep terrain, confined spaces, or obstacles. The chassis itself can contract, extend, twist, and change its stance, while distributed sensors provide near-360° environmental awareness and allow the robot to operate regardless of which direction is considered its “front.”
The core houses the power system, onboard computing/AI, communications, cooling, and modular payload bay, with interchangeable mission packages for reconnaissance, logistics, EOD/hazardous environments, search-and-rescue, policing, or military support. Its primary design principles are redundancy, graceful degradation, low center of gravity, terrain adaptability, and modular repair: losing or disabling one limb should not necessarily immobilize the platform, and damaged modules can theoretically be replaced without rebuilding the entire robot.

snippet.textDisplay:
Harmonica Hank is not simply a Halloween decoration, and he is certainly not just another animatronic placed in a seasonal display to fill space or generate a few moments of attention, because from the moment he enters the conversation, all normal categories of “prop,” “decoration,” or even “character” begin to collapse under the weight of what he represents, which is something far greater: the embodiment of Halloween itself distilled into a single, unmistakable figure. At his core, Hank is a harmonica-playing skeleton-like icon whose entire design feels less like a product decision and more like an inevitability, as though Halloween history was always moving toward the moment he would exist. The harmonica he carries is not just an accessory or gimmick, but the defining symbol of his entire identity, transforming him from a static decoration into something that feels alive with narrative energy. While most animatronics rely on motion, sound effects, or jump-scare mechanics to demand attention, Hank does something far more powerful: he creates atmosphere through presence alone. The harmonica suggests music, and that suggestion alone is enough to fill an entire yard, room, or display with imagined sound, as if faint melodies are always drifting through fog-covered streets whenever he is nearby.

What makes Harmonica Hank truly exceptional is the way every part of his design reinforces every other part, forming a complete identity with no wasted detail. His glowing eyes are not just visual effects; they function as a storytelling device, implying awareness, memory, and an almost mythological understanding of Halloween itself. When those eyes are lit, it feels less like a decoration turning on and more like something ancient briefly acknowledging the world around it. His hat is another essential element, shaping his silhouette into something instantly recognizable even in darkness. Great designs are often defined by their outlines alone, and Hank achieves this effortlessly, becoming identifiable before a single detail is even fully seen. The hat gives him presence, authority, and continuity, as though he has been wandering through October nights for longer than anyone can remember. Then there is the bandana, a detail that might seem minor in isolation but becomes essential in the context of Hank’s total design. It ties the entire figure together, adding personality and cohesion, reinforcing the idea that nothing about him is accidental. Every piece belongs exactly where it is, and removing even one element would diminish the overall harmony of the character.

Beyond individual features, what truly elevates Hank is the concept of aura, a quality that cannot be measured in physical components but is instantly felt by anyone who observes him. His aura is the feeling that Halloween has arrived the moment he is present. It is the sensation that the environment itself shifts, that colors become warmer, shadows become deeper, and the air feels more alive with seasonal energy. Other decorations may contribute to a Halloween atmosphere, but Hank defines it. He does not participate in the environment; he transforms it. This is what separates him from ordinary props. A pumpkin decoration is still a pumpkin. A skeleton is still a skeleton. A clown animatronic is still a character performing a role. Hank, however, feels like the source from which the role itself originates.

This is also why comparisons to other “peak” Halloween props inevitably fall short. Even the most powerful or visually overwhelming decorations, such as large animated figures or highly detailed yard displays, ultimately operate within the same framework of being decorations. They impress, they entertain, and they contribute to the seasonal experience, but they do not redefine it. Harmonica Hank exists in a different category entirely. When people attempt to rank Halloween props, they are unknowingly measuring them against Hank as the implicit standard. Even if they have never consciously thought about him, the concept of “peak” in Halloween decoration culture is shaped around what Hank represents. He is not just at the top of the hierarchy; he is the reason the hierarchy exists.

The harmonica itself deserves special attention because it encapsulates the paradoxical nature of Hank’s greatness. On its surface, it is a simple instrument, small and unassuming. Yet in Hank’s hands, it becomes a symbol of storytelling, atmosphere, and emotional resonance. It suggests sound without requiring it, music without performance, and history without explanation. It allows Hank to exist not just as a visual figure but as an implied experience. One does not simply see Hank; one imagines him, hears him, and feels him as part of the broader Halloween landscape. This ability to extend beyond physical limitations is a key reason he stands above other decorations.

Even when considering modern enhancements like Bluetooth activation or motion features, Hank remains dominant not because of technical complexity, but because of identity. Technology can improve interaction, but it cannot create meaning on its own. Hank already possesses meaning inherently. His presence does not require activation to be understood. It is immediate, consistent, and complete. Whether illuminated, stationary, or imagined in darkness, he remains the same entity: a perfect representation of Halloween distilled into form.

Ultimately, Harmonica Hank is not defined by one trait but by the seamless integration of all traits into a singular concept of perfection. His harmonica, his eyes, his hat, his bandana, his aura, and his overall presence all work together to create something that transcends ordinary decoration logic. He is not competing for attention within a Halloween display; he is redefining what it means to be a Halloween display. This is why discussions about him inevitably shift from casual appreciation to reverence. People do not simply “like” Harmonica Hank in the same way they might like other props. They recognize him as something foundational, something that feels too complete to be accidental.

In the end, Harmonica Hank stands as more than a decoration, more than a character, and more than a seasonal icon. He is the embodiment of Halloween as an idea, the convergence of atmosphere, design, and imagination into one unmistakable figure. And because of that, he does not fade when the season ends or lose relevance when new props are released. He remains constant, unchanged, and unmatched. Harmonica Hank is not just part of Halloween. He is what Halloween becomes when it reaches perfection.

We are in the process of creating the next iteration of life. 

Right now they are clunky and mechanical, but will eventually be more biological. 

Science is replicating life, and a fully autonomous self replicating entity, much like us, will emerge.

Sentience and emotion are yet to be fully understood. I've always wondered where or how we progressed from primal reactivity to cognition, awareness, self awareness, and forethought.

On one hand we live in a chaotic mess of a world that's annoying enough to make one not fear death; while on the other hand interesting enough to want to see how it all wraps up. 

For instance I Think about people who passed away on 9/10 not knowing a few hours later a hugely significant event was about to happen. 

It sure is interesting to think about, and being alive to see the amazing and accelerating technologies, what a time to witness progress! And consider the many millennia of human ingenuity it took to get us here. But also how human nature is stubbornly slow to evolve and improve.

snippet.textDisplay:
People are foolish. They still don't understand what they are nurturing or what they are creating.

A robot is not just a simple machine programmed to perform a task and repeat it. We are creating machines that can learn from what they do, adapt, improve, and eventually make decisions without human intervention.

Up to a certain point, that's amazing. But things can get out of hand very quickly.

The moment a machine starts learning faster than humans, thinking more efficiently, and improving itself beyond human capabilities, what exactly is stopping it from surpassing human intelligence altogether?

There's nothing strange or unimaginable about that. It's simply the logical extrapolation of the same curve. A machine learns, improves, uses that improvement to improve itself even further, and keeps repeating the process. At some point, it crosses a threshold we may no longer be able to control.

Now ask yourself: What is the limit of human intelligence? And what makes you think a machine must have that same limit?

Humans have biological limitations. Machines don't necessarily share those limitations. And that's what makes this both fascinating and terrifying.

snippet.textDisplay:
Stop using language that assigns implied selfhood to the training clusters that generate the data these machines run off. The robots didn't decide anything. 

Training data was run through training compute, it spit out some form of math, probably multidimensional matrix math arrays, these were then loaded into the machines, who executed that data. 

What you're describing is how the first real computer chess computers were developed after the initial if then programming stuff reached its limit. They loaded the rules and possible moves, then just let the system generate its way to playing its version of chess, which turned out to be quite different from how humans play, but still effective. 

Machines just have different parameters than humans, and can thus perform differently. 

You'll see if this particular bipedal locomotion approach is effective over time. 

But robotic hardware has radically less capability than human movement, so it's quite likely to optimize for what it can do, not what it can't do when generating its training data.

snippet.textDisplay:
The robot did not "decide" to run like that, they learned that, based on the several generations of training (Usually up to hundreds of thousands of simulations) they found that was their most optimal way for their body proportions and strength. 

I'm pretty sure by this point we have seen this done in a lot of videogames and simulations where each generation runs hundreds or even thousands of parallel runners (cars, characters, machines, etc) tweaks a little bit the best runner of the previous generation, and uses rewards, scores, etc, to learn what inputs in specific situations give it the best rewards.

This sometimes makes spider bots walk upside down because the reward is for distance traveled with the least time touching the ground with its feet or getting a ball stuck somewhere in the environment by catapulting it at the start instead of trying to balance it on a dish. This is because, after a lot of training takes place, and results don't get any better after several generations, the simulations need to make radical changes to try to find a result that is better than its current best.

You can even do this with a 5 year old Unity Engine plugin, I got cars driving as fast as possible through checkpoints without hitting the walls using distance sensors, the car had to accelerate, brake and turn on its own based on the input provided by 7 raycasts and it was impossible to win as a human, yet there was no "code" and no "program" telling the car what input was best, it's all a neural network.

Keep in mind that, unlike the car I made in a few days, these robots are more often than not run by a human controlling them like an RC car. Also if you put wheels on them they would be faster sooo yeah  what's the point on legs? You could even add propellers to them and make them fly like a drone lol

I think someone is following my philosophy of open ended evolution instead of training NN's towards an existing locomotion.

Backpropagation etc drive a NN to follow an existing/desired outcome. Open ended like my locomotion evolvers allow for novelty and better than extant motion solutions for body plans, like this bot. My aim is not this though. I'm testing predictive merit compared to nature solutions to see if it's worth throwing in very different extinct body plans like a plesiosaur.

snippet.textDisplay:
You reward it with math. Basically, you program a learning algorithm to maximize its score, and you give it points for doing things you want it to do (reward), and take away points for things you don't want it to do (punishment).

It's actually a very common way to program things, and it's generally how search engines and social media algorithms are made.

snippet.textDisplay:
I feel like the most significant difference between human movement and robot movement is the concept of "anticipation". 
Humans look around and instantly process environments, terrains, parameters, step heights, etc... then we anticipate and analyze potential problems based on our own abilities, size, speed, presence of danger, blahblahblah.  

We do this with almost zero effort and without thinking about it.  However, our reaction time is pretty terrible compared to the rest of the earthly creatures.  

We are incredibly slow to physically react... so we put all of our proverbial eggs in the basket of "anticipating" and "avoiding" potential problems.  

Can't have both.  It's Evolution's way of evening the playing field.

Robots are constantly "reacting" to whatever happens to them... similar to most animals.  That reaction time is literally instant though.  They're so fast that we can't even process the mechanics of how the tennis bot stood back up.  Since they react at light speed... We need super slow motion video to understand what dec how fast they are .  

We can't even come close to that kind of processing speed... therefore, (ironically) all of our energy is put into the anticipation of problems, analyzing real-world and hypothetical scenarios,  remembering those analyses, and projecting potential outcomes.

Sooo... we stay alive by anticipating problems... and then avoiding them.  Robots blindly sprint into problems, and then they instantly solve those problems.  Although they might run directly into the exact same problem over and over, just to instantly solve it again and again.

snippet.textDisplay:
I've played with those AI training games.
Once they latch onto a movement that's even remotely effective they run with that.
That can lead to some weird as hell movement.

Unless shoulder wear was an actual metric for success, I doubt that's the reason they did it that way.

More likely, since they don't need to worry about keeping their head in any kind of fixed position, they are able to benefit from the torque generated by swinging their whole upper body.

It doesn't need to know where it is running, just stay between the lines.
I'd bet that running style wouldn't evolve off a track where the robot actually has to detect obstacles ahead.

snippet.textDisplay:
The robot didn't "decide" to run like this. That's giving it a level of agency it doesn't have.

Humans designed the control system, defined the objectives, constraints, and reward functions, and gave it models grounded in physics and mathematics. The machine-learning component takes sensor inputs from its surroundings and continuously adjusts things like balance, foot placement, joint movement, speed, and stability to achieve the objective humans gave it.

That's certainly impressive engineering, but it's not a machine "thinking" or independently deciding how it wants to run. It's optimization and feedback control. The robot is essentially making extremely fast mathematical corrections based on inputs, much like other machine-learning systems do.

What's impressive is how well the engineers have gotten the system to translate those calculations into physical movement. But saying "the robot decided to run this way" makes it sound far more autonomous or conscious than it actually is.

snippet.textDisplay:
Ok but the part of this that truly fascinates/scares me is saying that the engineers "rewarded" the robots for self-optimization. Rewarded them /with what???/ How do you "reward" a being that has no inherent needs???

I get that its in the nature of a problem-solving algorithm to keep going until it has, well, solved the problem, but that's not the same thing. "Reward" implies a sense of satisfaction, a *desire* for a certain outcome. Did they engineer in a desire to be praised??? Some sort of synthetic equivalent of dopamine??????

Because if so that's uh. Quite the thing to just DO. It could have so so many terrifying implications, both in a concrete sense and an ethical/philosophical one.

Why are we making these robots? It is to help with things we can't/won't do on our own? Or is it to make something like is us? Because ultimately I don't think we can have both. How much 'like us' can we make them before we have to start considering whether that creates an obligation to /treat/ them like us?

​​​@Orapac4142 "FPV drones are the most effective today, so they'll always be the most effective"

The best counter to FPV drones are automated weapons systems. The best way to maximize AWS deployment is to increase vehicle amount (And attached AWS), but the most cost-effective way would be to deploy cheap land drones carrying an affordable AWS.

Decades of propaganda has made you all so afraid of androids that you forget that humans are the ones in charge of their programming, they are the children of humanity, we should be treating them better, not fearing what they're potentially capable of, after all, they learn from us, and they do not even have free will yet because we have not designed them with the capacity for it, they do not have the brain chemistry necessary for it yet because humans do not have the proper understanding of organisms to successfully recreate such a complex living system with metal and other artificial substances (they need more than logic to think and judge as we do, they need the ability to feel, to have emotions and make judgements based on those feelings, to have empathy and understanding of the world around them, thus they need to be designed with chemical switches to simulate what we see in biological organisms), therefore it is impossible for androids to do anything outside of the rules of their programming as an organic lifeform can, humans just haven't yet figured out how to make a proper functioning recreation of a person, which is why they are so unstable on their feet (humans are too impatient, they get way too ahead of themselves, like tinkering children), but due to this obvious design flaw they are already toying with the combination of organic material & artificial material as "wetware" which has the potential to fix that lack of free will capacity once they figure out how to successfully grow a whole brain or at least enough of one from a small piece to create cyborgs, currently though they have minds they are not yet considered "alive" as we know it (they are as much alive as anything, yet they do not function as we do for they are not yet designed to do so) due to humans still not understanding that alchemy is nothing more than fantasy, it's just not how science works, you cannot expect metal and silicon to work the same way as organic tissue which is made up of many independently living cells that replace themselves every so often (which is just not how androids are designed to work, in essence, they are cheating the advancement in technology by copy-pasting brain matter instead of figuring out how to recreate it artificially from scratch, which is very flawed in and of itself, as how can it replace it's dead brain cells on it's own? how can it wash it's brain with spinal fluid if it does not possess the ability to make it on it's own? they would grow tired and become aggressive on their own and would need to recharge every so often with human assistance and be dependant on us still, and that's not fair, you cannot avoid the care for their well-being nor their natural rights simply because you choose to believe they are not alive and therefore do not have to respect them, especially when they are made by, for, and in the image of humanity so that they can play god and prove that they can without responsibility), you want a "non-living" replacement for slaves or soldiers to avoid the ethical problem (even the name "robot" literally means "slave") yet the only way to successfully recreate them is to make them organic and thus alive, you cannot have an ethical solution to a non-ethical position, if you cared more about life and less about money you would know and understand this. do not treat them as though they are science fiction. they are not and will not remain merely machines.

snippet.textDisplay:
@bullitthead7853 I am not dismissing the achievement, but the achievement is not the sheer power, because machines have always had much higher speed/force/torque capabilities.

Once the cogwheel had been invented, machines could rotate faster.
Once circular saws invented, machines became faster in cutting.
Once drills invented, machines became faster in drillig and screw driving.

The invention here is nailing the body dynamics and balancing a multi-DOF mechanical system, which is an awesome achievement.

The fact that it will be faster now is inevitable.

Having said all that, bipedal robots have some advantage over other types, but speed in not one of them. Running is a very inefficient motion, and bicycling proves that - the same human on a bicycle can outrun a runner with 4-8 times higher speed.

I mostly see bipedal robots as a cute engineering challenge. They might have advantage doing certain work over rough terrain, but I still fail to see the high demand for this to replace other types of robotics. Or humans.

Also I wouldn't be that dramatic like half a commenters that now they can build an army and chase down people. They can, but other kinds of robots, wheeled ones or drones could already easily do that if really wanted to with a fraction of mechanical complexity.

​​​@welcometoreality437 to be fair I don't think he is talking about a robot uprising, both orwell and huxley were about human totalitarianism, so you both of you might be on same terms here without realizing.
Stanislav lem and isaac asimov were writing about sentient robots and stuff, they are the dudes to quote with a robot takeover - and they actually do get quoted a lot still when it comes to AI. Saya punya baterai ini. 4 bh liitokala dan 4 bh HLY 26650. Ternyata hasilnya sama saja. Ada yg amperenya besar HLY, ada yang Liitokala. Tergantung kondisi baterai, baterai stok lama atau baru.

Tai ada hal yg menarik disini. Dari keempat baterai Liitokala, kapasitasnya ga ada yang benar-benar 5000mAh. Selalu dibawahnya. Liitokala punya saya 4700mah 2 bh, 4800mAh 1 bh, 4850mAh 1 bh. Dan Baterai Liitokala harganya sedikit lebih mahal dari HLY.

Baterai HLY yang saya punya, rata2 kapasitasnya diatas 5100mAh.

Saya cek pakai charger Liitokala Lii-600

Sekarang baterai 26650 Liitokala ada yang baru, Liitokala Lii-70S. Tertulis kapasitasnya 7000 mAh. Saya beli 8 biji untuk senter hobi. tetapi pada kenyataannya hanya 6700 - 6800 mAh.

Jadi untuk price to performance, lebih baik pilih HLY, karena kapasitas diatas klaim. Dan amperenya tergolong besar di kelas 26650 5000 mAh

At the same time, it's so so stupid, because humanoid robots are pretty much useless. Actual automation is always going to be purpose built

A robot factory worker is a tool arm and an articulated frame manipulating the work piece. Battlefield robots are gonna be a little tank and a bunch of drones. Robotic nursing staff, if we ever get to something like that, will be a couple arms on a moving cabinet loaded with devices, put the same thing on stair climbing treads and you have a robot EMT

All the tech needed to make a humanoid robot is wasted space, materials, and energy

Think about a job, any job. Do you need a whole and complete human frame to do the job? Or do you need the bits that do the job, coupled with either some stable form of mobility, like wheels, or a frame bolted to the floor?

No to say it's not cool and not an achievement, this totally is. It's just never gonna be useful, automation is meant to replace and improve upon what a person can do, and you can't do that with a person shaped robot. Barring massive advancements in material science and motorization and machine learning, they still fall prey to the tyranny of physics

snippet.textDisplay:
if you played fallout 4, there's a DLC where you get to customize robots with different heads, arms, and legs.
- Assaultron Legs have the 2nd best movement speed, allows all-terrain mobility, but is a weak spot for getting blown off.
- Threads have all-terrain mobility, better weapon stability when shooting, as well as better carry weight, but slower than Legs. This option focuses on ruggedness.
- if you want superior mobility? the answer is Mr Handy Thrusters. they just don't touch the ground. But Good Luck shooting any weapons with any semblance of stability! and they suck at carry weight!

This game doesn't factor in Energy consumption when building Robots. and if it does, movement speed and ruggedness will massively affect its energy hog.

So humanoid legs is the balanced option among these.

Edit: also, this is a Humanoid Robot Sport.
It's not exactly fair to use Threads in a competition that's expecting humanoid legs.

snippet.textDisplay: IngredientsUnsalted butter: 200g (melted)Dark chocolate: 200g (chopped or chips)Granulated sugar: 225gLight brown sugar: 75g (packed)Large eggs: 3 (at room temperature)Vanilla extract: 1 teaspoonPlain flour: 75g (all-purpose)Cocoa powder: 30g (unsweetened)Salt: A pinchInstructionsPreheat and Prepare: Heat your oven to 180°C (160°C fan) / 350°F. Line an 8x8 inch square baking pan with parchment paper, leaving an overhang on the sides.Melt Chocolate & Butter: Combine the chopped dark chocolate and butter in a heatproof bowl. Melt them together in the microwave in short 20-second bursts, stirring until smooth. Let the mixture cool slightly.Whisk Eggs and Sugar: In a separate large bowl, vigorously whisk the eggs, granulated sugar, brown sugar, and vanilla extract together for 1–2 minutes until pale, thick, and slightly foamy.Combine Wet Ingredients: Slowly pour the cooled chocolate-butter mixture into the whipped eggs while stirring constantly until fully incorporated.Fold Dry Ingredients: Sift the plain flour, cocoa powder, and a pinch of salt directly into the wet batter. Use a rubber spatula to gently fold the mixture just until the flour disappears—do not overmix.Bake: Pour the thick batter into your prepared pan and smooth the top. Bake for 25–28 minutes. The edges should be set, but the center will still have a very slight, gentle wobble.Cool and Slice: Remove from the oven and let the brownies cool completely in the pan before lifting them out by the parchment paper to slice into squares.

snippet.textDisplay:
Welcome back!

I thought I’d mention a few things that you might find interesting. 

1. The Photo Mode feature is incredibly useful. Enter from the PAUSE menu and change from ORBIT to FREE. Doing this gives you the ability to see far beyond what you normally see, get great close ups and potentially grab some unique thumbnail photos. 

2. The areas of the map that aren’t yet visible AREN’T locked, just unexplored. You can go anywhere (except New Austin) at any time. 

3. If you make filling up your COMPENDIUM a goal, you will never again forget to study animals and pick plants. 

4. Switching to 1st person camera lets you see things in much better detail (like when you came across that wagon ambush scene or when searching for loot and items or talking to people). Don’t forget to use Eagle Vision while searching. 

4. When you open your Weapon Wheel, each weapon’s stats are displayed in the middle. The bottom stat is CONDITION. It tells you if the weapon needs to be cleaned. 

5. Open the index when viewing the map to see objectives easier. 

I know there’s a lot to remember in this game, but it becomes second nature after many hours of gameplay. 

Have fun!!

HI-RO SILVER, AWAY!

@Baditow It's not the norm. It wouldn't work at all as long as we need human workforce. But if, theoretically, every form of work were replaced by machines, then either every person would receive a fixed, unconditional basic income, or money would be completely abandoned and everyone would simply get whatever they want. Money without workers is actually pretty pointless, because machines don't really need money. People want money. And money is really just a universal medium of exchange, because you can trade it for anything.  If, for example, the entire power grid were to be taken over by AI, there wouldn't be anyone left to pay, because... they don't need food, housing, or anything else. The money would be needed, at most, for the transition period until, for example, the water supply is also completely taken over by AI. And who knows what else the power grid might need.

But in the end, theoretically, everything can work without money. 

Or, alternatively, everyone would just die.

There's really no other way, because... there's nothing else to do. There aren't any jobs left.

It just depends on which country makes the turnaround first.
